CHAPTER IV. Agbicultube and Forests. The tea industry has exhibited a markod develop- T<* indoi- ment in this district during the last decade. The area trJ- under tea has increased from 40,497 to 44,177 acres, and the total outturn of manufactured tea by About 70 per cent. Nearly all the available land to the north of the Trunk Road between the Belsiri river and the Sapoi road has been taken up and cleared for tea cultivation. Further west, in the Borchola and Orang mauzas, there have recently been numerous applications for special leases for land suitable for tea, and there can be little doubt that if the prospects of the industry continue good, a large proportion of the stretches of waste land in this part of the district will soon be brought undor cultivation. The area under jute also shows a marked tendency Jut*, to increase. The yield last year (1913-14) was # about 100,000 maunds. This crop is cultivated largely by Nepalis who have settled in the district, particularly in the Behali circle. Since 1905 the only addition to the reserved forests j M(rTC d has been a small area of 40 acres which was added to fowti.

the Gamiri reserve in 1913, Proposals for an addition 2 to the Charduar reserve, and also for the formation of a new reserve in the north-east of the district and of game reserves in Gohpur and Orang mauzas are now under the consideration of Government. CHAPTER VI. Economic condition of ihe people. Wsfti ind As in other districts in the province prices of rice and P"” 1, other food stuffs have shown a steady tendency to increase during the past ten years. This has been accompanied by a corresponding riso in the rate of wages of the labouring classes. The average daily wage of a day labourer is now eight annas as compared with five or six annas some ten years ago. At the same time the question of an adequate supply of labour is becoming one of increasing difficulty each year. Commmiet* Paring the last three or four years there has been a tioD». marked improvement in communications throughout the district. This is largely duo to the generous special grants recently given by Government for the purpose. In the sadr subdivision a new road has been constructed linking the Balipara road with tho Sootia-Coldarghat road and having a ferry crossing at the Bharali. This road connects the Tczpur and Bishnath tea districts. Portions of the Charali-Biswanath, the Belsiri-Balipara and ihe North Trunk roads have been much improved by metalling. In tho north of tho Mnngaldai subdivision new roads have been constructed, connecting the stations on the Rangiya-Tongla extension of the Eastern Bengal State Railway with the tea gardens. The settled area in WT#BW - 1906-06 was 435,422 acres with a revenue demand of Es. 7,39,400. The area in 1913-14 had risen to 513,656 acres with a revenue demand of Rs. 8,60,076, showing an increase of 78,134 acres in area and of Rs. 1,20,676 in revenue. The rate of expansion has been continuously maintained except in 1909-10 when

there was a fall of Es. 6,074 in the revenue demand as oomparedwith the previous year. The decrease was more apparent than real, as the preparation of correct statistics in that year was complicated by the resettle- ment operations. The gradual increase is attributed to the expansion of ordinary cultivation brought about ebiefly by Nepali settlers, ear-garden coolies, and settlers from Mymeeaingb who have oocupied the riverain mauzas in the south of Mangaldai, princi- pally in connection with the cultivation of jute. 4 lieiM. The consumption was highest in 1908-09 when it amounted to 222 maunds. In the following two years there was a con* siderable drop, hut last year (1913-14) it rose again to 210 mounds. The habit is most widespread in the Mangaldai subdivision, where nearly all the Kacharis end lowor class Assamese are addicted to it. The habit of smoking the drug is said to be on the increase, and it is estimated that not less than half the consumers are smokers. In order to restrict the use of the drug the treasury price has been gradually raised from Us. 37 to Ks. 42 per seer, and the number of retail shops reduced from 98 in 1905-06 to 54 in 191M3. The outstill system was discontinued in 1908-09 and since then the oontract distillery system has been in fcice. The spirit is manufactured at Jorhat and is sent down to the Tezpur warehouse where it is reduced to strengths of 30 U. P. and 60 TJ. P. and issued to the

ritail vendors. Though the population has increased, consumption has remained nearly stationary and it is generally agreed that drunkenness is decreasing. Government sanctioned in 1912 the establishment of a new outpost at Dhckiajuli within the jurisdiction of Tezpur police station. This was necessary for the convenience of neighbouring villages and also on account of the new tea areas m Borcbola mauza. The outpost has not been opened yet, but the buildings are under construction. This dread disease appears to be gradually dying out in the district, though it is still fairly widespread in the Mangaldai subdivision. Tho number of deaths attributed to it decreased from 1,106 iu 1905 to 899 in 1913. The following is quoted from the report of the All-India Sanitary Conference of 1912-18 on kala-atar. " Tetpur subdivision .— There are only two villages which are certainly infected and 14 which .contain one or two very doubtful cases. The infection hee practically died out of the Tezpur subdivision. 6 " Pott kittory.—W o record is traoeable except the fad thatthere was some mortality from hala-atar in 1896 . "In IDaogaon Fukri which is one of the two undoubtedly infected villages the people state that during the epidemio of kala-atar the viotims died almost as suddenly as in a cholera epidemio. "The general opinion in the district ii that halo* atar has almost disappeared. This is also the opinion of the Conference. " It appears that propagation of iala-atar is in this way : An area gets infected by importation. The infeotion spreads and a panio is established. Infected families who have lost one or two of their numbers and see others dying decide to migrate elsewhere to an uninfected area. They do so, if unchecked, taking with them an infected person or the seeds of the disease. This leads to the propagation of the disease in this area and the process then repeats itself."

CHAPTER IV. Agbicultube and Forests. The tea industry has exhibited a markod develop- T<* indoi- ment in this district during the last decade. The area trJ- under tea has increased from 40,497 to 44,177 acres, and the total outturn of manufactured tea by About 70 per cent. Nearly all the available land to the north of the Trunk Road between the Belsiri river and the Sapoi road has been taken up and cleared for tea cultivation. Further west, in the Borchola and Orang mauzas, there have recently been numerous applications for special leases for land suitable for tea, and there can be little doubt that if the prospects of the industry continue good, a large proportion of the stretches of waste land in this part of the district will soon be brought undor cultivation. The area under jute also shows a marked tendency Jut*, to increase. The yield last year (1913-14) was # about 100,000 maunds. This crop is cultivated largely by Nepalis who have settled in the district, particularly in the Behali circle.
